title: Three perfect days in Prague: the castle, the river and the young wine
dek: The week after St. Martin's Day, when the new wine and roast goose take over the Vltava embankment, two museums open new shows and the opera houses are full.

hero.caption: Prague Castle above Malá Strana, where Friday begins with the cathedral and ends over roast duck below the hill.

intro:
Mid-November is a good time to have Prague mostly to yourself. The summer crowds are gone, the Christmas markets have not arrived, and the city is still celebrating St. Martin, whose feast on November 11 brings out the first young wine of the year and a week of roast goose. On Saturday the season's big party, the St. Martin's festival on the Náplavka embankment, runs from 10:00 to 20:00, with free entry. Smaller goose festivals follow on Sunday in Karlín.

Two shows open on Friday: the second chapter of *Memory of Touch* at Kunsthalle Praha, and *Jewish Museum: 120 Years* at the National Museum. The National Gallery's large exhibition on Queen Anne Jagiellon, marking 500 years since the Habsburgs took the Bohemian throne in 1526, fills the Wallenstein Riding School. The National Theatre's three stages have Tosca, Onegin and La traviata. The Czech Philharmonic is away on tour in Spain, so the Rudolfinum is quieter than usual.

This plan takes Friday in the castle district and Malá Strana, Saturday on the river from Vyšehrad to the National Theatre, and Sunday in Vinohrady and at the top of Wenceslas Square. Days are short and often gray: it is dark by about 16:30, so each day keeps the walking for the morning and moves indoors in the afternoon. One thing to know if you are staying on: Tuesday, November 17, is a public holiday, Struggle for Freedom and Democracy Day, with free commemorations on Národní třída.

days.title: Friday: the castle and Malá Strana
days.intro: Up the hill early, before the tour groups, then down through the palaces of Malá Strana to two new exhibitions and a duck dinner.

stops.name: Café Savoy
stops.text: Begin under the painted Neo-Renaissance ceiling of Café Savoy, a grand café from 1893 at the Malá Strana end of the Legion Bridge. It is known for breakfast and its pastry counter: order eggs, which come several ways, or one of the set breakfasts, and take a pastry from the cases by the bar. **Practical:** it opens at 08:00 on weekdays; book for a table at weekends, and check the bill, since service may already be included. Tram 22 from the Újezd stop nearby climbs to the castle in about fifteen minutes.

stops.name: Prague Castle and St. Vitus Cathedral
stops.text: The castle complex is the largest sight in the city, so pick a circuit. Circuit B (250 CZK) covers the essentials: the historic part of St. Vitus Cathedral with the Wenceslas Chapel, the Old Royal Palace, St. George's Basilica and Golden Lane. The front, neo-Gothic part of the cathedral is free. **Practical:** in winter the buildings are open 09:00 to 16:00, so arrive early; the Great South Tower opens at 10:00 and closes in bad weather. Tickets are valid for two days, which helps if you want to come back.

stops.name: Kuchyň
stops.text: Lunch is next to the castle gates, in the Salm Palace on Hradčanské náměstí, where Kuchyň ("kitchen") cooks Czech classics drawn from old palace cookbooks and pours a careful Pilsner. The schnitzel with potato salad is the dish to order, and the yeast dumpling filled with plum butter is a proper Czech dessert. The terrace looks over the roofs of the whole city. **Practical:** open daily from 12:00; you order and pay upstairs, and in summer the garden seats go fast.

stops.name: Anne Jagiellon at the Wallenstein Riding School
stops.text: Walk down the Old Castle Stairs to the National Gallery's exhibition of the season. *Anne Jagiellon (1503–1547): Queen at the Dawn of a New Era* marks 500 years since the Habsburgs came to the Bohemian throne, and tells it through a queen who traveled constantly and had fifteen children. More than 200 loans, from Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum, Berlin and Kraków's Wawel, include work by Cranach, Dürer and Titian. **Practical:** open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00, until March 28.

stops.name: Kunsthalle Praha
stops.text: Five minutes away at Klárov, Kunsthalle Praha opens the second chapter of *Memory of Touch* today, and its curator, Tevž Logar, leads a tour at 18:00. Upstairs, *Tragikomedie* is a large show of the French artist Annette Messager, running until February. One ticket (320 CZK) covers everything. **Practical:** Kunsthalle stays open until 21:00 on Fridays and closes on Tuesdays. The café terrace faces Petřín and the castle, which is worth a look as the lights come on.

stops.name: U Modré kachničky
stops.text: Dinner is at the Little Blue Duck, behind a painted duck above the door of a 16th-century house on a quiet Malá Strana lane. The rooms are full of antique furniture and hand-painted murals, and the kitchen does Czech country cooking: roast duck, and game in season, which in November is the time for it. **Practical:** open daily 12:00 to 23:00; book by phone, as the small rooms fill on Friday nights.

days.title: Saturday: Vyšehrad and the river
days.intro: The old fortress in the morning, the St. Martin's festival on the embankment for lunch, and ballet at the National Theatre.

stops.name: Café Louvre
stops.text: Café Louvre has been open at Národní 22 since 1902, and it still has a billiard room at the back. Come for a Czech breakfast, such as pancakes or a small breakfast goulash, and come back another day for the apple strudel. **Practical:** it fills up later in the morning, so come early. Trams 2 and 17 run south along the river from Národní divadlo toward Vyšehrad, and the walk along the embankment takes about 30 minutes.

stops.name: Vyšehrad
stops.text: Prague's other castle is a hilltop fortress with ramparts over the Vltava. Walk past the Rotunda of St. Martin, one of the oldest buildings in the city, to Vyšehrad Cemetery, where Dvořák, Smetana, the Čapek brothers and Mucha are buried beside the Basilica of St. Peter and St. Paul. Under the walls, the Baroque casemates lead to Gorlice Hall, where several original statues from Charles Bridge are kept. **Practical:** casemate tours start at the Brick Gate; check times on the Vyšehrad website. The cemetery and ramparts are free.

stops.name: St. Martin's Festival on Náplavka
stops.text: Walk down from the fortress past Josef Chochol's Cubist apartment houses (1912–14) to Rašínovo nábřeží, where the St. Martin's festival fills the embankment from 10:00 to 20:00. Winemakers pour this year's young wines, the *svatomartinská vína*, and stalls sell roast goose, red cabbage and dumplings. **Practical:** entry is free; you pay for tastings and food. Go before 14:00 if you want a seat at the tables by the water, and bring a warm layer, as the riverside gets cold.

stops.name: Dancing House
stops.text: At the north end of the embankment stands the Dancing House by Vlado Milunić and Frank Gehry, the pair of towers locals call Ginger and Fred, which turns 30 this year. The gallery inside is open 09:00 to 19:00 (230 CZK). Afterward, take the lift to the Glass Bar for a coffee or beer and the view up the river to the castle as the light goes, which is around 16:30. **Practical:** the gallery ticket does not cover the bar, and the outdoor balcony has cost extra in 2026.

stops.name: U Fleků
stops.text: Beer has been brewed on this site since 1499, and U Fleků still pours only its own dark lager, brought round on trays to the long tables. Under the dark wood and vaulted halls, order roast pork with dumplings or sausages; this week there is also a St. Martin's goose menu (until November 15), if the festival has not already covered goose for you. **Practical:** open daily 10:00 to 23:00. It is touristy and loud with musicians, which is half the point. It is ten minutes on foot to the National Theatre.

stops.name: Onegin at the National Theatre
stops.text: The National Theatre's ballet company dances *Onegin*, the ballet after Pushkin's novel in verse, in the gilded 19th-century house on the river. Even if ballet is not your thing, it is a good way to see the auditorium and the painted curtain. **Practical:** there are shows at 14:00 and 19:00. When we checked, the evening show had only a few tickets left and the matinee more, so book now. At the State Opera the same night, *Nabucco* starts at 18:00 with English surtitles.

stops.name: Forbína
stops.text: End the night across the street in Forbína, the cocktail bar that took over the old Café Slavia space in the Lažanský Palace in 2024. The menu follows the theater opposite, in sections for ballet, drama, opera and Laterna Magika; Swan Lake comes in a swan-shaped glass. In June it won Best Cocktail Bar in Czechia at the Bartenders' Choice Awards. **Practical:** cocktails have run about 300 CZK and cards are accepted. We could not confirm closing time, so check before you set off; nearby Hemingway Bar is the backup.

days.title: Sunday: Vinohrady and Wenceslas Square
days.intro: A neighborhood morning in Vinohrady, the National Museum's new show, and an early opera.

stops.name: Dos Mundos
stops.text: Vinohrady is where Prague lives, a grid of Art Nouveau apartment houses with a café on most corners. Dos Mundos, on Sázavská, roasts its own specialty coffee and serves breakfasts from around the world: Turkish eggs, or the plate it calls the Breakfast of Champions. It also pours natural wine, if you want to start Sunday that way. **Practical:** open on Sundays from 09:00 to 18:00. It does not take bookings, so if it is full, the cafés around náměstí Míru are a short walk away.

stops.name: Havlíčkovy sady (Grébovka)
stops.text: Walk ten minutes south to Havlíčkovy sady, which locals call Grébovka: a 19th-century park laid out around a Neo-Renaissance villa, with a terraced vineyard on the slope. In November the vines are bare, but the paths are quiet and the views run across Nusle to Vyšehrad, which you climbed yesterday. **Practical:** the park is free and open all day. The paths are steep and can be slippery after rain, so wear proper shoes. If it is pouring, go straight to the museum instead.

stops.name: Pho Vietnam Anglická
stops.text: Prague has a large Vietnamese community, and some of the best everyday food in the city is theirs. This basement noodle room near náměstí Míru is a local favorite for beef pho; the menu also has a long vegan list, including crisp tofu in tomato sauce. It is a warm, quick lunch between a cold walk and the museum. **Practical:** open daily 11:00 to 22:00. It is a short walk from náměstí Míru and about fifteen minutes on foot from the National Museum.

stops.name: National Museum
stops.text: The National Museum's Historical Building closes the top of Wenceslas Square. Inside, see the domed Pantheon and the main staircase, then the new exhibition, *Jewish Museum: 120 Years*, which opened on Friday. Also on are *Maps and Atlases from the Kinsky Library* and a show on the composer Jaroslav Ježek. Outside, the memorial to Jan Palach and Jan Zajíc is worth seeing two days before November 17. **Practical:** open daily 10:00 to 18:00; one ticket (360 CZK) covers the whole complex.

stops.name: La traviata at the State Opera
stops.text: The State Opera is a three-minute walk from the museum, a gilded 19th-century house that is part of the National Theatre. Verdi's *La traviata* starts at 17:00 with English surtitles, so you are out in time for a late dinner. It is a good first opera, and a good place to hear one. **Practical:** buy through the National Theatre's programme page; when we checked, tickets were still available. Leave coats in the cloakroom.

stops.name: Kantýna
stops.text: Dinner is five minutes away in Kantýna, a butcher's shop and meat restaurant in a former bank in the Ringhoffer building. You order at the counter, from cuts of Czech beef and pork to the burger many people come for, and the butchers will also sell you meat to take home; the beer is poured at a separate bar. **Practical:** open until 22:00 on Sundays, so do not linger at the opera. It takes no reservations, and the beer bar is cash only.

stay.name: Mandarin Oriental, Prague
stay.text: A 14th-century convent on a quiet lane below the castle, a few doors from U Modré kachničky, so Friday is all on foot. Rooms have vaulted ceilings, and the spa sits over the ruins of a medieval church that you can see through a glass floor, which suits a cold November afternoon. The restaurant is Monastiq.

stay.name: Hotel Paris Prague
stay.text: A neo-Gothic hotel with Art Nouveau interiors, built in 1904–07 next to the Municipal House and protected as a national cultural monument. Bohumil Hrabal set part of *I Served the King of England* here, and it now holds two Michelin Keys. It is a 15-minute walk to the National Museum and the State Opera on Sunday.

stay.name: Dancing House Hotel
stay.text: Rooms inside Gehry and Milunić's Dancing House, on the embankment where Saturday's St. Martin's festival takes place and ten minutes' walk from the National Theatre. Ask for a river view: some rooms face a busy road junction instead. The Glass Bar on the roof is open to guests and visitors until 22:00.

events.name: Memory of Touch: Chapter II opens
events.text: The second chapter of Kunsthalle's *Memory of Touch* opens, with a tour led by its curator, Tevž Logar. Annette Messager's *Tragikomedie* runs alongside it.

events.name: Jewish Museum: 120 Years
events.where: National Museum, Historical Building, Wenceslas Square
events.text: A new exhibition on the 120 years of the Jewish Museum in Prague opens at the National Museum and runs until May 31, 2027.

events.name: Tosca
events.text: Puccini's *Tosca* at the State Opera, with English surtitles.

events.name: James Lisney piano recital
events.text: The British pianist gives a recital in the Rudolfinum's small hall, the main concert there this weekend while the Czech Philharmonic tours Spain.

events.name: St. Martin's Wine Festival and Roast Goose
events.text: The city's largest St. Martin's party: young Czech wines, roast goose and stalls along the river. Free entry.

events.name: Onegin
events.text: The National Theatre ballet in *Onegin*. The evening show was nearly sold out when we checked.

events.name: Karlín goose festival (Karlínská husa)
events.text: An open-air goose and young-wine festival on the square in front of the Church of Sts. Cyril and Methodius, with music and stalls. Free entry.

events.name: La traviata
events.text: Verdi's *La traviata*, with English surtitles; an early start that leaves time for dinner.

know: **From the airport:** bus 59 runs from Václav Havel Airport to Nádraží Veleslavín (metro line A) and bus 100 to Zličín (line B); allow 35 to 45 minutes to the center, on an ordinary 90-minute ticket (46 CZK in the app). The Airport Express (AE) to the main station costs 200 CZK and passes are not valid on it. A taxi, Uber or Bolt usually takes 25 to 40 minutes.

**Transit:** buy tickets in the PID Lítačka app, where they are cheapest: 36 CZK for 30 minutes, 46 CZK for 90 minutes, 140 CZK for 24 hours, 340 CZK for 72 hours. Paper tickets cost a little more and must be validated once when you first board.

**November 17:** Tuesday is Struggle for Freedom and Democracy Day, a public holiday marking the student protests of 1939 and 1989. Korzo Národní fills Národní třída with free music and exhibitions from 10:00 to 20:00, and the National Gallery's permanent collections are free that day.
**Closed days:** the National Gallery, including the Wallenstein Riding School, closes on Mondays; Kunsthalle Praha closes on Tuesdays. Prague Castle's buildings close at 16:00 in winter.
**Short days:** it is dark by about 16:30. Do the walks in the morning, and bring a warm layer and an umbrella.

**Money:** the currency is the Czech koruna (CZK). Cards and phone payments work almost everywhere, but carry some cash for festival stalls and beer bars. If a card machine offers to charge you in your home currency, decline.

**Tipping:** round up or add about 10 percent in restaurants and cafés, unless service is already on the bill, which some cafés do. Tell the server the total you want to pay when they bring the card machine.
